subject: Critical Thinking
title: Premises and Conclusions: The Building Blocks
description: Learn Premises and Conclusions: The Building Blocks in one minute.

hook.text: Every argument has the same skeleton: some statements support another statement. That's it.

buildup.text: The supporting statements are premises. The statement they support is the conclusion.

discovery.text: 'All cats are mammals. Whiskers is a cat. Therefore, Whiskers is a mammal.' Two premises, one conclusion.

twist.text: Most real-world arguments hide their premises. Advertisers and politicians are masters at this.

climax.text: Finding hidden premises is the single most powerful critical thinking skill you can develop.

punchline.text: Before you accept a conclusion, find what it's standing on.

quiz.question: What are the supporting statements in an argument called?

details.summary: Every argument consists of premises—the supporting statements—and a conclusion—the claim being argued for. Identifying which is which is the essential first step in evaluating any argument's strength.
details.whyItMatters: Many arguments hide their premises or disguise conclusions as facts, and recognizing the structure is the key to seeing through this.
takeaways: Premises provide the evidence or reasons
The conclusion is the claim the argument supports
Indicator words like 'therefore' and 'because' signal structure

faq.question: How can you identify the conclusion of an argument?
faq.answer: Look for indicator words like 'therefore,' 'thus,' 'so,' and 'consequently.' The conclusion is the statement everything else is trying to support.

faq.question: Can an argument have more than one premise?
faq.answer: Yes, most arguments have multiple premises that work together to support a single conclusion. Each premise contributes part of the evidence or reasoning.
